title: Dates and time zones with Intl
when: The app shows, stores or compares dates and times, schedules across time zones, or dates appear one day off.
inputs: which values are instants and which are calendar dates
prompt:
Goal: Instants stored as UTC ISO strings, calendar dates kept as YYYY-MM-DD, and every display formatted by Intl in the right zone.
Steps:
1. Classify each value: an instant (created at, meeting start) stored with toISOString(), or a calendar date (birthday, due date) stored as "2026-10-17".
2. Display instants with cached Intl.DateTimeFormat(locale, { dateStyle: "medium", timeStyle: "short", timeZone }).
3. Read the user zone with Intl.DateTimeFormat().resolvedOptions().timeZone and store it with events tied to local time.
4. Build local dates from parts with new Date(y, m - 1, d); new Date("2026-10-17") is UTC midnight and can show the previous day.
5. Add days with setDate(getDate() + n), not 86400000 ms steps that break on daylight saving changes.
6. Relative labels with Intl.RelativeTimeFormat; in HTML use <time datetime>.
Quality bar:
- Dates read naturally in the user locale.
- A due date never shifts when the user travels.
- Tests run under a fixed TZ and cross a daylight saving day.
Pitfalls:
- Local time strings stored without offset.
- Comparing date strings in different formats.
- Hand written month name arrays.
Verify:
- [ ] Instants stored in UTC ISO.
- [ ] Calendar dates as YYYY-MM-DD.
- [ ] Formatting through Intl.DateTimeFormat.
- [ ] A daylight saving test.
Output: js/dates.js with parse, format and date math helpers, and its tests.

examples.input: a data de vencimento aparece um dia antes
examples.output: store due as "2026-10-17", build with new Date(y, m-1, d), format via Intl.DateTimeFormat pt-BR
